warmup.q: A producer with default settings sends a payment, and the Future fails with a TimeoutException after delivery.timeout.ms. What do you know about the payment?
options: It was not written: the producer gave up before the broker stored it
It may or may not be in the log
It is in the log exactly once, because idempotence is on by default
It is in the log, but marked as failed so consumers skip it
warmup.why: The timeout means the producer stopped waiting, not that the broker never wrote the record. A request can be appended and its answer lost, or processed by a stalled broker after the producer gave up; the Try-it in this lesson shows four such payments. Idempotence prevents duplicates from the producer's own retries, but it can't tell you whether this record made it. Kafka has no "failed" marker on records.

sections.h: send() puts the record in a batch and returns
sections.html:
Your payment service emits 20,000 events a second at peak. If every send() became its own request and waited for its answer, two things would go wrong. A round trip to a broker in the same data centre takes about half a millisecond, so one thread waiting for each answer manages about 2,000 sends a second. And the broker would handle 20,000 requests a second, each with its own headers, checks and disk append, for records of a few hundred bytes. Most of its work would be overhead.

The producer avoids both with one design: send() doesn't send anything. (Every default in this lesson is the Kafka 4.4 producer's.) It does three things on your thread and returns:

  1. It serializes the key and the value into bytes.
  2. It picks the partition (lesson 5 of this track).
  3. It appends the record to a batch for that partition, in a buffer called the record accumulator, and returns a Future<RecordMetadata>.

A separate thread inside the producer, the sender, does the network work. It takes batches that are ready (the next section says when), groups them by the broker that leads their partition, and sends one produce request per broker carrying batches for many partitions at once. When the answer comes back, it completes each record's Future and runs its callback.

So the return of send() means "queued", not "written". You learn the outcome from the Future or the callback:

Java
producer.send(record, (metadata, e) -> {
    if (e != null) log.warn("payment {} not confirmed", id, e);   // runs on the sender thread
});
Kotlin
producer.send(record) { metadata, e ->
    if (e != null) log.warn("payment {} not confirmed", id, e)     // runs on the sender thread
}

Calling send(record).get() on every record throws the design away: your thread waits for each answer, and each batch carries one record. Use the callback, or keep the futures and check them later. flush() waits until everything queued so far has an answer, and close() does the same before it shuts down.

send() can still block, in two cases. The first send to a topic waits for its metadata, which says how many partitions it has and who leads them. And when the accumulator's memory, buffer.memory (32 MiB by default), is full because the brokers are slower than your code, send() waits for space. Both waits end after max.block.ms, one minute by default, with an exception. The producer is thread-safe, and the KafkaProducer javadoc says one instance shared by all threads is generally faster than several, because their records share batches.

sections.h: A batch leaves when it is full or when linger.ms runs out
sections.html:
The sender needs a rule for when a batch may leave. Sent too early, it carries one record. Held too long, every payment waits. Kafka uses two settings, per partition.

batch.size is the most a batch may hold: 16,384 bytes by default. When the next record doesn't fit, the batch is closed and may leave at once.

linger.ms is how long a batch may wait for more records: 5 ms by default. A batch that is 5 ms old may leave even if it holds one record. Until Kafka 4.0 the default was 0, meaning "send as soon as the sender is free". The producer docs give the reason: the efficiency of bigger batches usually makes latency similar or lower overall, despite the wait.

Put numbers on it. At 1,000 records a second for one partition, a record arrives every millisecond. With linger.ms=5, each batch collects about 5 records before it leaves. With 50, about 50, and each record waits up to 50 ms longer. A burst behaves differently: when 170 records of 100 bytes arrive at once, 163 fill a batch to 16 KB, and that batch leaves at once without waiting. Step through both below.

linger.ms=0 doesn't mean one record per request either. The producer keeps up to 5 requests in flight per broker connection (max.in.flight.requests.per.connection). When they are all waiting for answers, new records pile up in the accumulator and leave together in the next request. So under heavy load batches form anyway; linger.ms matters most at moderate traffic, where the sender would otherwise send small batches as fast as it can.

Batches are also where compression happens. With compression.type set to lz4, zstd, snappy or gzip, the producer compresses each batch as one unit. The broker stores the compressed batch as it arrived (the topic's default compression.type=producer means "keep what the producer sent"), and the consumer decompresses it. Payment events repeat the same field names and currencies, so they compress well, and bigger batches compress better because there is more repetition to find. The Try-it measures all of this from the producer's own metrics.

try.title: Measure batching from the producer's own metrics
steps: From the labs folder, start the broker with docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait, then create a one-partition topic: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic ledger-events --partitions 1.

Predict the records per request for linger.ms 0, 5 and 50 at about 1,000 records a second. Then run the demo (command below). It sends 500 payment events per setting and prints four producer metrics: records-per-request-avg, batch-size-avg, compression-rate-avg and record-queue-time-avg.
Keep the broker running for the next Try-its.

import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** * Sends 500 small payment events to "ledger-events" at about 1,000 a second, once per setting, * and prints what the producer's own metrics say about its batches. */ public class BatchingDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("linger.ms compression records/request bytes/batch compressed/raw batch waited (ms)"); run(0, "none"); run(5, "none"); run(50, "none"); run(50, "lz4"); } static void run(int lingerMs, String compression) throws Exception { Map<String, Object> config = Map.of( "bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092", "key.serializer", StringSerializer.class, "value.serializer", StringSerializer.class, "linger.ms", lingerMs, "compression.type", compression); try (var producer = new KafkaProducer<String, String>(config)) { List<Future<RecordMetadata>> acks = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 500; i++) { String event = "{\"id\":\"pay-" + i + "\",\"account\":\"acct-" + i % 50 + "\",\"amount\":4000,\"currency\":\"EUR\"}"; } } /** One value from the producer's "producer-metrics" group. */ static double metric(KafkaProducer<String, String> producer, String name) { return producer.metrics().entrySet().stream() .filter(e -> e.getKey().group().equals("producer-metrics") && e.getKey().name().equals(name)) .mapToDouble(e -> (Double) e.getValue().metricValue()) .findFirst().orElseThrow(); sections.h: Retries happen on their own, inside one deadline: delivery.timeout.ms
sections.html:
Lesson 4 of this track covered what the leader waits for before it answers. With acks=all, the default since Kafka 3.0, it waits until every in-sync replica has the batch. With acks=1 it answers once its own copy has it. With acks=0 the producer doesn't wait for any answer, so it never learns an offset (the metadata says -1) or an error.

Answers can be errors. Some are retriable: the condition may pass if the producer tries again. NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER (the leader moved), NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS (lesson 4's ISR floor) and a request that timed out are all retriable. Others are not: a record bigger than the broker allows, or a missing permission, fail the send at once.

For retriable errors the producer retries on its own. retries defaults to 2,147,483,647, in effect forever, with a pause between attempts that starts at 100 ms and doubles up to 1 second. Each attempt waits at most request.timeout.ms, 30 seconds by default, for its answer.

"Forever" is bounded by one setting: delivery.timeout.ms, 2 minutes by default. It starts when send() returns and covers everything after: the time in the batch, the wait for a free request slot, every attempt and every pause. When it runs out, the producer fails the record with a TimeoutException. The producer requires it to be at least linger.ms plus request.timeout.ms. The docs advise leaving retries alone and setting this deadline instead.

Now the part that matters most for payments. A TimeoutException tells you the producer gave up waiting. It doesn't tell you the record is missing. Picture the request that reached the broker, was appended, and whose answer was lost, or a broker that stalled with your request in its socket buffer and processed it after the producer had given up. The Try-it below does exactly that: it pauses the broker for 8 seconds while payments flow with a 5-second deadline. Five sends fail, and four of those five are in the log anyway.

So a failed send means unknown, not "not written". Code that treats it as "not written" and sends the payment again, or reports it as failed to the customer, gets it wrong some of the time. Retry it with the same idempotency key, and let the consumer drop the duplicate. Lesson 7 of this track builds that consumer.

try.title: Stall the broker past the deadline
steps: Open a second terminal in the labs folder and type, without pressing Enter: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml pause kafka; sleep 8; docker compose -f env/kafka.yml unpause kafka. pause freezes the broker's process without closing its connections.
In the first terminal, run the demo with a 5-second deadline (command below). It sends pay-00 to pay-29, one every 500 ms. When pay-10 appears, press Enter in the second terminal.

Read the failures and the last line. Then list the records written around the pause; use the offset of the last fast record before the failures (2015 in the run below): docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic ledger-events --partition 0 --offset 2015 --max-messages 8 --formatter-property print.offset=true.

sections.h: Retries duplicate and reorder; the idempotent producer stops both
sections.html:
Retries create two problems of their own. The first is duplicates. If the leader appended a batch and the answer was lost, the retry is appended again, and the leader can't tell a retry from a new record. The second is reordering. With 5 requests in flight, request 1 can fail while requests 2 to 5 succeed. When request 1 is retried, its records land after the others. A capture overtakes its authorization within one partition, which breaks the one order lesson 5 promised.

The simplest fix for reordering is one request in flight at a time. That works, and it caps each broker connection at one round trip per batch. Kafka's fix keeps 5 in flight and fixes duplicates too: the idempotent producer, added in Kafka 0.11 and on by default since 3.0.

At start-up the producer gets a producer id from the broker. It numbers the records it sends to each partition 0, 1, 2 and so on, and every batch carries the producer id and the sequence number of its first record. For each producer the leader remembers the next sequence it expects and the last 5 batches it appended. Then:

  • a batch with the next sequence is appended;
  • a retry of one of the last 5 batches is a duplicate: the leader writes nothing and answers with the offset it gave the first time;
  • anything else is a gap. The leader refuses it with OUT_OF_ORDER_SEQUENCE_NUMBER, and the producer resends the missing batch first.

You have seen this idea before. The Encoding track's lesson on calling other services made a retried request safe with an idempotency key: the client sends the same key with every retry, and the server remembers which keys it has already handled. The idempotent producer is that, built into Kafka's protocol. The key is the producer id plus the sequence number, and the leader is the server that remembers, for the last five batches.

That explains the three requirements: acks=all, retries above 0, and max.in.flight.requests.per.connection at most 5. Five is the number of batches the leader can recognise (ProducerStateEntry.NUM_BATCHES_TO_RETAIN in the broker). acks=all makes sure an acknowledged batch, with its producer id and sequence, is on every in-sync replica, so a new leader rebuilds the same state from its copy of the log.

The requirements have a trap. If you set a conflicting value, such as acks=1 for speed, and don't mention enable.idempotence, the producer turns idempotence off silently. No warning, and duplicates and reordering are back. If you set enable.idempotence=true yourself, the same conflict is a ConfigException at start-up. So set it explicitly in every payment producer. The lab checks both behaviours on a real broker.

Know where the guarantee stops. It covers retries made by one producer instance, inside its delivery timeout. When your code catches a TimeoutException and calls send() again, that is a new record with a new sequence number, and it is written twice if the first one made it. A restarted service gets a new producer id. Duplicates across those boundaries need the application's own idempotency key, the one from the Encoding track, carried in the event and checked by the consumer; lesson 7 of this track builds that consumer.

refs.title: Kafka 4.4 design: the idempotent producer and delivery semantics

video.title: A lost answer, a retry, and the idempotent producer

analogy: Think of the post room of a company. You drop a letter in the tray for its city and walk away: that's send() returning. A clerk empties each tray when the bag is full or when the van leaves every five minutes, whichever comes first: batch.size and linger.ms. Registered mail gets a receipt, and if the receipt doesn't come back, the clerk sends the letter again. With idempotence, every letter carries a sender number and a running number, and the receiving office throws away a second copy of a number it already has. The analogy breaks at the end: a letter the clerk gave up on may still be delivered, and the receiving office remembers only the last five bags from each sender.
world: In your Quarkus payment services, make three producer settings explicit: enable.idempotence=true, so a later change to acks fails at start-up instead of quietly allowing duplicates; acks=all; and a delivery.timeout.ms you chose, shorter than the Temporal activity timeout that wraps the send, so the activity sees the producer's answer before it gives up itself. Treat a failed send in that activity as "unknown": let Temporal retry the activity, send the same event with the same idempotency key, and make the consumer drop duplicates. Raise linger.ms to 10 or 20 ms and turn on lz4 for high-volume event topics such as ledger-entries, and check batch-size-avg and record-queue-time-avg before and after.
mistake: Treating a TimeoutException from send() as "the payment was not sent" and sending it again under a new id, or telling the customer it failed. The exception only says the producer stopped waiting; the record may well be in the log, and the resend then charges or books it twice. People make this mistake because an exception usually means "nothing happened". The fix has two parts: the retry reuses the same idempotency key (not a new event id), and the consumer ignores a key it has already applied. The idempotent producer can't help here, because a second send() is a new record.

compare.title: A payments producer with its safety settings stated, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: KafkaProducer<String, String> producer = new KafkaProducer<>(Map.of( ProducerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, bootstrap, ProducerConfig.KEY_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringSerializer.class, ProducerConfig.VALUE_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringSerializer.class, ProducerConfig.ENABLE_IDEMPOTENCE_CONFIG, true, // a conflicting setting now fails at start-up ProducerConfig.ACKS_CONFIG, "all", ProducerConfig.LINGER_MS_CONFIG, 10, ProducerConfig.COMPRESSION_TYPE_CONFIG, "lz4", ProducerConfig.DELIVERY_TIMEOUT_MS_CONFIG, 60_000)); // at least linger.ms + request.timeout.ms producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("payments", accountId, eventJson), (md, e) -> { if (e instanceof TimeoutException) outcome.complete(Outcome.UNKNOWN); // maybe written: retry with the same key else if (e != null) outcome.complete(Outcome.FAILED); else outcome.complete(Outcome.WRITTEN); });

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: val producer = KafkaProducer<String, String>( mapOf( ProducerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG to bootstrap, ProducerConfig.KEY_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG to StringSerializer::class.java, ProducerConfig.VALUE_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG to StringSerializer::class.java, ProducerConfig.ENABLE_IDEMPOTENCE_CONFIG to true, // a conflicting setting now fails at start-up ProducerConfig.ACKS_CONFIG to "all", ProducerConfig.LINGER_MS_CONFIG to 10, ProducerConfig.COMPRESSION_TYPE_CONFIG to "lz4", ProducerConfig.DELIVERY_TIMEOUT_MS_CONFIG to 60_000, // at least linger.ms + request.timeout.ms ), ) producer.send(ProducerRecord("payments", accountId, eventJson)) { md, e -> outcome.complete( when (e) { null -> Outcome.WRITTEN is TimeoutException -> Outcome.UNKNOWN // maybe written: retry with the same key else -> Outcome.FAILED }, ) }

compare.note: Both pass a Map to the constructor; Java's Map.of takes up to ten pairs, which fits here. The callback's e is null on success. Kotlin's when (e) with is TimeoutException reads as one decision table, where Java needs an instanceof chain. TimeoutException here is org.apache.kafka.common.errors.TimeoutException, not the one in java.util.concurrent. The outcome future is yours: something like a CompletableFuture<Outcome> the calling code waits on.

worked.title: Choose linger.ms from your traffic, then check it

steps.say: ledger-entries takes 20,000 events a second at peak over 12 partitions, about 1,700 a second per partition, or one every 0.6 ms. Events are about 300 bytes. With the default linger.ms=5, a batch collects about 8 events, about 2.4 KB, far below batch.size. Filling 16 KB would take about 55 events, about 33 ms. The ledger consumer's latency budget is 200 ms, so linger.ms=20 costs little: about 33 events, 10 KB, per batch.
Measure instead of trusting the arithmetic. Read the producer's own metrics after a few minutes of real traffic. producer-metrics is the group with the producer-wide averages.
steps.code: // average over the producer's metric window (30 s by default) double metric(KafkaProducer<?, ?> p, String name) { return p.metrics().entrySet().stream() .filter(e -> e.getKey().group().equals("producer-metrics") && e.getKey().name().equals(name)) .mapToDouble(e -> (Double) e.getValue().metricValue()) .findFirst().orElseThrow(); }

alt.html: // average over the producer's metric window (30 s by default) fun KafkaProducer<*, *>.metric(name: String): Double = metrics().entries.first { it.key.group() == "producer-metrics" && it.key.name() == name } .value.metricValue() as Double

steps.say: Log the four numbers that describe batching: records per request, bytes per batch, compression ratio and how long batches waited.
steps.code: log.info("records/request {} bytes/batch {} compressed/raw {} waited {} ms", metric(p, "records-per-request-avg"), metric(p, "batch-size-avg"), metric(p, "compression-rate-avg"), metric(p, "record-queue-time-avg"));

alt.html: log.info("records/request {} bytes/batch {} compressed/raw {} waited {} ms", p.metric("records-per-request-avg"), p.metric("batch-size-avg"), p.metric("compression-rate-avg"), p.metric("record-queue-time-avg"))

steps.say: Read them. If batch-size-avg sits near 16,384, batches fill before linger.ms ends: raise batch.size (32 or 64 KB) before you touch linger.ms. If record-queue-time-avg is close to linger.ms and batches are small, traffic is light and the wait buys little: lower it. A compression-rate-avg of 0.3 means the network and the brokers' disks carry 30% of the raw bytes.

lab.title: Model the accumulator and the leader's duplicate check
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. 15 of 20 fail. The 5 that pass are in ProducerOnBrokerTest and need no code from you: they read a real producer's metrics and ask a Kafka 4.4 broker which producers it tracks (Admin.describeProducers). One of them proves that acks=1 silently turns idempotence off.
In BatchAccumulator.kt, write append: use the partition's open batch if the record fits, otherwise close it and start a new one at nowMs; close a batch once it reaches batchSize.

In IdempotentLog.java, write append in the order of its javadoc: a remembered batch is a Duplicate, the expected sequence is Appended, anything else is OutOfOrder. Keep at most BATCHES_TO_RETAIN remembered batches.
Run everything until all 20 pass. Then reread the test with five batches in flight and say why the leader may refuse batches that arrive early.
hints: In append, queue.lastOrNull()?.takeIf { !it.closed } is the open batch, if any. A record larger than batchSize goes into a fresh batch, which is then closed at once because it is already full.
drain must stop at the first batch of a partition that may not leave yet: a younger batch behind it can't overtake it.
Check for a duplicate before checking the sequence: a retry's base sequence is lower than the expected one, so the gap check would refuse it.

drill.title: Be the leader
drill.prompt: Producer 7's last five batches on this partition covered sequences 0 to 9 (two records each), so the leader expects 10 next. What does it answer to each of these, arriving in this order: (a) base sequence 10, 2 records; (b) base sequence 8, 2 records; (c) base sequence 14, 1 record; (d) base sequence 0, 2 records? Then write the decision as code in Java or Kotlin.

answer.html: // (a) Appended: 10 is expected; next becomes 12, remembered batches are now 2-3 .. 10-11 // (b) Duplicate: 8-9 is still remembered; answer with its original offset, write nothing // (c) OutOfOrder(12): a gap, 12 and 13 are missing; write nothing // (d) OutOfOrder(12): 0-1 was the oldest batch and was forgotten when (a) arrived for (BatchInfo b : state.recent) { if (b.firstSeq() == baseSequence && b.lastSeq() == lastSeq) return new Duplicate(b.baseOffset()); } if (baseSequence != state.nextSeq) return new OutOfOrder(state.nextSeq); // append, remember the batch (keep 5), move nextSeq past it, return Appended

alt.html: // (a) Appended: 10 is expected; next becomes 12, remembered batches are now 2-3 .. 10-11 // (b) Duplicate: 8-9 is still remembered; answer with its original offset, write nothing // (c) OutOfOrder(12): a gap, 12 and 13 are missing; write nothing // (d) OutOfOrder(12): 0-1 was the oldest batch and was forgotten when (a) arrived state.recent.firstOrNull { it.firstSeq == baseSequence && it.lastSeq == lastSeq } ?.let { return Duplicate(it.baseOffset) } if (baseSequence != state.nextSeq) return OutOfOrder(state.nextSeq) // append, remember the batch (keep 5), move nextSeq past it, return Appended

recap: send() serializes, picks the partition and appends to a batch in the accumulator, then returns a Future. A sender thread sends ready batches, one request per broker.
A batch leaves when it is full (batch.size, 16 KB) or old enough (linger.ms, 5 ms since Kafka 4.0). Compression works per batch, so bigger batches compress better.
Retriable errors are retried automatically until delivery.timeout.ms (2 minutes) runs out; then the send fails with a TimeoutException.
A failed send means unknown, not unwritten: the record may be in the log. Retry with the same idempotency key and dedupe at the consumer.

The idempotent producer (default since 3.0) is an idempotency key built into the protocol: producer id plus sequence numbers. The leader drops retried duplicates and refuses gaps, so retries neither duplicate nor reorder.
Idempotence needs acks=all, retries > 0 and at most 5 in-flight requests. A conflicting setting turns it off silently unless you set enable.idempotence=true yourself.

explain.prompt: A junior engineer asks: "We have idempotence on, so we can never get duplicate payments in Kafka, right?" Explain what idempotence does, how, and where it stops.
explain.answer: It stops one kind of duplicate. When the producer retries a batch because the answer got lost, the leader would normally append it again. With idempotence the producer has a producer id and numbers every record per partition, so the leader sees the same producer id and sequence on the retry, recognises it among the last five batches it remembers, writes nothing and returns the original offset. Gaps are refused too, so retries can't reorder records either. But it only covers that producer's internal retries. If our code gets a TimeoutException and calls send again, that is a new record with a new sequence number, and if the first one made it we have two. A restarted service also gets a new producer id. So we still put an idempotency key on every payment and the consumer skips keys it has already applied. And someone setting acks=1 without enable.idempotence=true would turn it off silently, so we set it explicitly.

deeper.html:
Look at the dump from the 5-second-deadline Try-it, if you kept the broker: the batches after the failures say producerEpoch: 1 and their sequence numbers start again at 0. When a batch expires, the producer can't know whether the leader appended it, so its sequence numbers might now have a gap the leader would refuse forever. Since Kafka 2.5 (KIP-360) the idempotent producer handles this by bumping its epoch, a counter next to the producer id, and starting its sequences again at 0; the leader accepts sequence 0 from a newer epoch. Lesson 10 of this track uses the same epoch to fence a zombie transactional producer; since Kafka 4.0 (KIP-890), transactional producers bump it on every transaction.

Two more settings change the picture. max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=1 keeps order without idempotence, at the cost of one round trip per batch to each broker; with idempotence there is no reason to lower it. The producer docs advise keeping request.timeout.ms (30 s by default) larger than the brokers' replica.lag.time.max.ms (also 30 s): with acks=all, a slow follower can hold an answer back for up to that long, and timing out earlier only adds retries and, without idempotence, duplicates. The Try-its used 2 s only to make the stall visible quickly.

Finally, acks=0. The producer sends and forgets: no answer, no offset (the metadata says -1), no retries that could help, and idempotence is off. It fits metrics or debug events you can afford to lose, never payments.
